## **Cloning your repo:**

***Docker & WSL Warning:*** Both Docker and WSL are notorious for eating up storage over time. When running your ROS server, every once in a while you should check on how much storage Docker and WSL are taking up on your computer. You can look up (or ask your favorite AI tool) how to clean up space/cache that these both build up, just be wary not to delete containers you or your friends plan on using.

***If you are on a Windows computer:*** Install WSL. When you clone any repos, make sure they are cloned when you are in WSL.

- Check if you have permissions to create a branch on this repo: [https://github.com/h2r/spot\_ros2\_multi\_ws](https://github.com/h2r/spot_ros2_multi_ws)  
  - If you have permissions, SSH clone this repo and create a separate branch from main  
  - If you do not have permissions, fork the repo and SSH clone your forked repo  
    - On your forked repo, create a separate branch from main. This way when you submit a pull request to the H2R repo, it will already be on a separate branch from main  
  - *If the computer you are cloning on is giving issues with SSH cloning* use HTTPS cloning instead. HTTPS cloning means when you push your changes, you will be prompted for a username and password each time, so try to eventually switch your upstream from HTTPS to SSH. You can look up how to do this (or ask your favorite AI tool).  
- The ros workspace has subrepos, you’ll have to run “git submodule update –init –recursive”  
  - You will likely run into an error about “correct access rights”, meaning you need your ssh key. You can look up how to make a new SSH key (or ask your favorite AI tool)   
  - If you get issues with public keys and permission denied, there’s a chance you haven’t configured your username and email or someone else’s username and password is configured instead. You can run “git config –global user.name” to see the name.   
  - If you run into “WARNING: UNPROTECTED PRIVATE KEY FILE\!” You will have to create a secure SSH directory inside WSL so you can access it.  
    - Run “mkdir \-p \~/.ssh” then “chmod 700 \~/.ssh”.  
    - Copy the keys from Windows into Linux. This means copying the locations of your keys, so you would run “cp /mnt/c/\<location here\>/.ssh/id\_ed25519 \~/.ssh/id\_ed25519” and “cp /mnt/c/\<location here\>/.ssh/id\_ed25519.pub \~/.ssh/id\_ed25519.pub”. \<location here\> would be something like “Users/user1234” or wherever the SSH key is saved.  
    - Now you need to lock down your file permissions. Run “chmod 600 \~/.ssh/id\_ed25519” and then “chmod 644 \~/.ssh/id\_ed25519.pub”  
    - Finally, run “ssh \-T [git@github.com](mailto:git@github.com)”. Now it should say: Hi \<github username\>\! You’ve successfully authenticated, but GitHub does not provide shell access.  
    - Now that you’re authenticated, you can run “git submodule update –init –recursive”

## **Configuring Docker:**

***Reminder\!*** If you are on Windows, make sure you are in WSL when following the next steps

- Enter your cloned repo (type cd \~/spot\_ros2\_multi\_ws into the terminal)  
- To avoid annoying issues later, I highly recommend adding “pip3 install bosdyn-client bosdyn-mission bosdyn-api bosdyn-choreography-client aiortc” to your dockerfile if it is not already there. When you run the ROS server later, it will expect these packages (yes, including the choreography one regardless of if you’re paying for the subscription for it…)  
- Install Docker Desktop on your computer if you do not have it  
  - It is also possible to have Docker running natively inside your WSL terminal, but this tutorial will use Docker Desktop  
- To run docker, open the docker app  
  - If on Windows, you need to configure Docker with WSL. Go into settings → resources → WSL Integration. Enable integration with default WSL distro and additional distros. Apply these changes and restart. You then need to open a brand new WSL terminal and go back into spot\_ros2\_multi\_ws.  
- If prompted in VSCode, download container tools  
- Type “docker compose up \-d”  
  - When running this for the first time, it should start to build your container and take some time. When you run this command in the future, it will start your container much quicker since it’s already been built.  
- Once “docker-compose up \-d” works without issues, run “docker-compose exec ros2\_ws bash”  
- You are in the container, congrats\! Now go to **starting your ROS server**


Possible Issues:

- If Docker fails while building and you fix the issue (e.g., you forgot to download the subrepos)  
  - Run “docker compose up \-d –build”, this will make Docker rebuild the image  
- If Docker says “unknown shorthand flag: ‘d’ in \-d”, try quitting Docker, then typing “exit” to get out of WSL and typing “wsl –shutdown”. Open a new terminal and reopen WSL and go back into spot\_ros2\_multi\_ws. Now try docker compose up \-d \--build.  
- If the above still gives “unknown shorthand flag: ‘d’ in \-d” and invalid plugins, you need to wipe broken Docker plugins inside of WSL. Run “ls \-la /usr/local/lib/docker/cli-plugins/” to see the broken files.   
  - If you see broken files or an error, you need to delete the contents in that folder so Docker is forced to rebuild them. Run “sudo rm \-rf /usr/local/lib/docker/cli-plugins/\*”  
  - Do into the Docker Desktop and uncheck the WSL integration → Apply & Restart → Reselect the WSL integration options → Apply & Restart  
  - Open a new WSL terminal, and retry  
- sudo cp /usr/local/lib/docker/cli-plugins/docker-compose /usr/local/bin/docker-compose   
- If there are still issues: run “docker-compose up \-d \--build”. This runs a legacy command which should bypass the issues above.  
- Still issues even after the above? Run “sudo curl \-SL https://github.com/docker/compose/releases/download/v2.26.0/docker-compose-linux-x86\_64 \-o /usr/local/bin/docker-compose” and then run “sudo chmod \+x /usr/local/bin/docker-compose”  
  - Try running “docker-compose version”. If it prints a version, then run “docker-compose up \-d \--build”

Possible NVIDIA Issues:

- If you get Error response from daemon: could not select device driver "nvidia" with capabilities: \[\[gpu\]\]  
  - Run this: curl \-fsSL https://nvidia.github.io/libnvidia-container/gpgkey | sudo gpg \--dearmor \-o /usr/share/keyrings/nvidia-container-toolkit-keyring.gpg \\ && curl \-s \-L https://nvidia.github.io/libnvidia-container/stable/deb/nvidia-container-toolkit.list | \\ sed 's\#deb https://\#deb \[signed-by=/usr/share/keyrings/nvidia-container-toolkit-keyring.gpg\] https://\#g' | \\ sudo tee /etc/apt/sources.list.d/nvidia-container-toolkit.list  
  - Run “sudo apt-get update” then “sudo apt-get install \-y nvidia-container-toolkit”  
  - Now run “sudo nvidia-ctk runtime configure \--runtime=docker”. If you get something like “config file does not exist” this is ok, now run “sudo service docker restart”  
  - Finally, run “docker-compose up \-d”. If there were no NVIDIA issues, this means the graphics card was successfully bridged\!  
- If you get E: Unable to locate package nvidia-container-toolkit  
  - Run this: echo "deb \[signed-by=/usr/share/keyrings/nvidia-container-toolkit-keyring.gpg\] https://nvidia.github.io/libnvidia-container/stable/deb/amd64 /" | sudo tee /etc/apt/sources.list.d/nvidia-container-toolkit.list   
  - Then continue from “sudo apt-get update” above

## **Starting Your ROS server:**

- Run “./launch\_multi\_spot\_ws.sh”  
  - If you’ve been working on Windows, you’ll have Windows characters that will mess with running this launch (you’ll get an error like: /bin/bash^M: bad interpreter). Do these following steps:  
    - apt-get update && apt-get install \-y dos2unix  
    - dos2unix ./launch\_multi\_spot.sh   
    - chmod \+x ./launch\_multi\_spot.sh   
    - Now, try running “./launch\_multi\_spot\_ws.sh”  
    - If dos2unix doesn’t work, try “sed \-i 's/\\r$//' ./launch\_multi\_spot.sh” then running “./launch\_multi\_spot\_ws.sh”  
- Now, multiple terminal windows should open. What you likely will see is that packages are not being found. You need to let your environment know that ROS2 packages exist (explained below).  
  - You can exit the terminal windows by pressing Ctrl+B then pressing D. This leaves the windows running the background, which you can get to again by typing “./launch\_multi\_spot.sh”. To terminate all of the windows, type “tmux kill-server” in the container.  
- To let the container know above the ROS2 packages, you need to build them by running the following:  
  - 1.) Pull ROS dependencies automatically  
    - rosdep update  
    - rosdep install \--from-paths src \--ignore-src \-r \-y   
  - 2.) Compile the workspace (this step may take long the first time, anywhere from 10 to 35 min to even longer since it heavily depends on the PC)  
    - colcon build \--symlink-install   
  - 3.) Source the workspace  
    - source install/setup.bash   
- Finally, run “./launch\_multi\_spot.sh”  
- All terminal windows should work except for the first two, which should say “Configuration file for …./spot-tusker.yaml does not exist” and similarly for spot-gouger. We will fix this in the steps below:  
  - Go into spot\_ros2\_multi\_ws → src → spot\_multi → config\_examples  
  - Here, you should see spot\_tusker.yaml and spot\_gouger.yaml  
  - ***IMPORTANT:*** Do not share the below info when filled out to ANY AI tool when you need help.  
  - Copy these yaml files into the secrets folder and fill in the files with the necessary info. I will not be listing it here for privacy reasons, so you’ll have to ask someone in the lab.  
  - Now, rerun “./launch\_multi\_spot.sh” (kill the old terminals with tmux if they’re still up)  
- Docker issues: container not appearing in the GUI in docker desktop  
  - Need to go in task manager → kill every docker process \-\> open up docker desktop again → docker compose up \-d → should build then run docker compose exec ros2\_ws bash  
- Switch the IPs in Unity to your machine’s IP, both in the Inspector and in the ThreadedRosConnector and RosConnector scripts. There’s around 25 prefabs in Unity that have the aforementioned scripts attached, so rather than changing them in the Inspector manually you could run the ghost.unity file through an AI tool and have it switch them for you (make sure Unity is completely closed while doing this and double-check that nothing else in the file was changed besides the IPs).  
  - If you are doing this on the same computer as Unity, write 127.0.0.1 as your IP address

## **Networking Shenanigans:**

- Despite this *supposed* to be working now, you might find that Unity and the ROS server are not talking to each other. To fix this, you’ll need one more step which is opening your ports.  
- Comment out “network mode: host” in your dockerfile  
- Add a port mapping in the dockerfile like so:

  ports:

- "9090:9090"   
- Run “docker compose down \--remove-orphans” in the terminal, then “docker compose up \-d \--force-recreate \--build “  
- Go onto Docker Desktop and make sure 9090:9090 is appearing (you might have to click on the drop down on the container)  
- Networking is hard (citation needed), so your particular issue means you need to google/ask an AI. Just make sure to not share sensitive information. When in doubt, make sure you’re able to talk to your ROS server through its port to make sure that is working. Then, make sure Unity is looking for the connection by looking at the console. Unity console messages are helpful (citation needed), so always look there to see what could be going wrong.  
  - One tip is that Unity might show it trying to connect to multiple IPs. Just make sure the IP of your ROS server is one of them. If it’s not, you need to go into the ROSConnector (maybe more than one) and see.

Congrats\! By now, your ROS server should be working and talking to Unity through a ROS bridge\!

- You need the map for the robots to localize. The lab should have a map folder that can be placed in the secrets folder. This folder needs to be in the secrets folder for the robots to localize via GraphNav
